This methodology is very 362 appropriate to detect the nature of shocks in a very flexible way permitting, for example,363    for nonstationary mean reverting behaviour with series having transitory though long-364 lasting effects. The application of fractional integration methods in this work is an 365 important methodological contribution in the sense that it outperforms the standard 366 methods based on integer degrees of differentiation, allowing for a higher flexibility in 367 the modelization of the series.368The results suggest an enormous degree of heterogeneity in the countries 369 examined. Nevertheless, some conclusions can be inferred from our results. We find 17370 countries where the order of integration is constrained between 0.5 and 1, implying 371 nonstationarity though mean reversion. Thus, the no applicability of the appropriate 372 differentation before conducting Granger causality test or ordinary least squares (OLS), may cause erroneous conclusions in the results. Moreover, the conventional diagnostic 374 statistics which are utilised to evaluate OLS estimates will suggest a statistically 375 significant relationship between the series when there is no relationship and ultimately 376 the procedure may yield inappropriate policy actions. Moreover, 77 out of the 90 series 377 investigated (85.5%) display a nonstationary pattern and more than half of them belong 378 to the upper-middle-and high-income levels. This is in line with the results provided in 379 Yilanci et al. (2019). On the other hand, 14.4% of the series appear to be stationary (with 380 an order of integration below 0.5), and most of the them belong to lower-middle-and 381 low-income countries. 382 A policy implication of the results is that there is a path dependence or hysteresis 383 in the fishing grounds footprint of the upper-middle-and high-income levels and therefore 384 shocks resulting from policies implemented to stem the fishing grounds footprint per 385 capita will have long lasting impacts on their growth, suggesting that policies aimed at 386 changing the path of the fishing grounds footprint will be effective. On the other hand, 387 the policies aimed at ensuring conservation of fishery resources and protecting essential 388 fish habitats, especially the fishing grounds footprint per capita in the lower-middle-and 389 low-income countries might not be effective. Policies that can protect fishing habitats 390 include regulating or prohibiting trawling and other forms of destructive fishing in 391 countries where these activities are common. There is also a need to improve institutional 392 arrangements for fisheries management in order to reduce fishing grounds footprint.
